metadata.title: ICT, Motivation, and Academic Performance in Elementary Education: Meta-analysis, Literature Review, and State of the Art

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This publication is a meta-analysis and systematic literature review based on 19 eligible studies (2019–2023) identified through Scopus and Web of Science searches following PRISMA guidance. It does not analyze ILSA microdata (e.g., PISA/PIRLS student responses) and therefore does not define a student-level sampling frame, complex survey design, or replicate-weight scheme. As a result, there are no ILSA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to apply, and no PV/scaling procedures are performed at the paper level. Any weighting, PV handling, or missing-data treatment would belong to the primary studies included in the review, not to this synthesis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a systematic review/meta-analysis of published studies rather than an empirical analysis of ILSA student microdata. Because the dependent variables are synthesized across heterogeneous primary studies (e.g., motivation/engagement and academic performance outcomes) and no PV-based cognitive achievement scores are generated or modeled within this paper, plausible-value handling is not applicable. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not fit a statistical model to an original dataset; instead, it reports inclusion/exclusion criteria and qualitative/quantitative synthesis of study findings.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Systematic review/meta-analysis following PRISMA (Page et al., 2021). Searches in Scopus and Web of Science (September 2023) using Boolean terms including “Motivation” AND “Education” AND “ICT”, plus title/abstract/keywords screening; duplicates removed via Mendeley. Inclusion criteria (PICO): primary/elementary education (and first cycle of secondary education), ICT used as a medium/tool for methodological improvement, outcomes providing innovative teaching practices applicable to primary classrooms, and language restricted to Spanish or English, with publication years 2019–2023. Exclusions: non-primary/first-cycle populations; ICT for non-educational entertainment; other languages; studies before 2019; clinical trials related to COVID-19 and e-learning platforms; and during full-text review, exclusions due to content mismatch, wrong educational stage, or restricted access. Final eligible set for the review/meta-analysis: 19 documents.

data.outcome_summary: This paper synthesizes evidence (2019–2023) on how ICT use in elementary/primary education relates to student motivation/engagement and academic performance. It follows PRISMA-based procedures and uses Scopus and Web of Science searches, yielding 19 eligible studies after screening and full-text eligibility checks. The results are reported as a predominance of positive associations in quasi-experimental studies (n=10) between digital resources, engagement, and academic performance, with stronger benefits when ICT is paired with active methodologies such as gamification, flipped classroom, or project-based learning. The review also highlights implementation conditions—digital resource design, teacher age, and lack of effective training—as determinants of whether ICT adoption translates into improved outcomes. Limitations include the small number of included studies and heterogeneity across interventions and measures, so effect sizes and causal claims cannot be directly inferred from this synthesis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction contains no student-level ILSA microdata analysis, no PV-based achievement modeling, and no ML training/evaluation. The paper is a meta-analysis/literature review that aggregates findings across 19 eligible studies, so fields such as total_students, country-level student counts, PV handling, missing-data handling for an analytic dataset, and ML techniques are not applicable to this synthesis-level design.
